# The Fractured American Common

The notion of an "American common"—a shared civic space where citizens gather in unified purpose—has always been more myth than reality. What we actually inhabit is not a collective in any meaningful sense, but rather a temporary convergence of private needs and pleasures that happen to overlap within public spaces. The soccer mom at the grocery store, the retiree at the pharmacy, the teenager at the mall—each pursues their own private agenda, their paths crossing briefly in shared physical space without ever coalescing into genuine communal identity. The commons, in other words, is less a gathering than a collision of separate orbits.

This fragmentation has not gone unnoticed by those with power and profit motives. Behind the visible transactions of daily life, powerful institutions operate with a kind of quiet calculation, treating ordinary people not as fellow citizens but as targets—witless marks to be studied, categorized, and ultimately exploited. Corporations, political operatives, and media conglomerates alike have learned that the fractured nature of the American public makes it uniquely vulnerable to manipulation. Where there is no unified "we," there are only segments to be pried apart and sold to.

The mechanisms for this exploitation are now remarkably sophisticated. Marketing systems and algorithmic sorting technologies have taken the messy, contradictory reality of human beings and flattened it into digestible categories: the soccer mom, the NASCAR dad, the urban millennial, the rural conservative. These labels serve a singular purpose—commercial and political targeting—reducing the vast diversity of individual human experience into narrow demographic niches that can be efficiently marketed to, persuaded, or manipulated.

Yet here lies the deeper problem: these categorizations, while containing kernels of statistical truth, are profoundly inadequate to the task of capturing actual human beings. Yes, certain purchasing patterns may correlate with certain demographics. Yes, algorithms can predict behavior with unsettling accuracy in aggregate. But the map is not the territory. These data-driven abstractions are so impoverished, so thin, that they fail catastrophically to represent the full complexity of any real person's inner life.

Consider the surgeon who spends her evenings playing poker with unexpected ferocity, revealing a competitive streak that no medical marketing algorithm could have predicted. Consider the plumber who disappears each weekend to fish quietly by the river, seeking a solitude that contradicts every blue-collar stereotype constructed for him. These individuals resist the tidy categories constructed to contain them. They remain irreducibly themselves—complicated, contradictory, and whole—existing not as data points but as full human beings living beneath a sky that remains, in the end, utterly indifferent to all our systems of classification. That sky offers no labels, no demographics, no targeted advertisements—only the vast, wordless silence beneath which every human being, in all their unmarketable complexity, quietly persists.
outputs.L4:
# The Reduction of the American Public

There is a peculiar violence done to human beings when they are sorted into marketing categories, though we rarely notice it because the sorting feels so natural, so data-driven, so *scientific*. Open any corporate strategy document, any algorithmic targeting model, any consumer profile database, and you will find Americans reduced to labels: baton twirlers, evangelical retirees, soccer moms, NASCAR dads, urban millennials with disposable income. These categories are not entirely wrong—that is what makes them so insidious. Somewhere there really is a woman who twirls batons on weekends and attends church twice on Sundays. The data is not fabricated; it is merely *incomplete* in a way that masquerades as completeness.

The algorithm does not lie about the baton twirler. It lies about what she *is*, which is to say, it lies by omission about everything else she contains. Perhaps she also nurses a private grief for a sister she has not spoken to in a decade. Perhaps she reads Russian novels in translation and has strong, half-formed opinions about the nature of time. Perhaps she is, in the deep architecture of her personhood, unclassifiable—not because she resists categories but because she exceeds all of them simultaneously, the way a symphony exceeds any single instrument's part.

This is the fundamental failure of demographic targeting: it mistakes the label for the territory. Consider the surgeon who plays poker on Thursday nights, bluffing with the same steady hands that hold a scalpel Monday through Friday. Consider the plumber who fishes at dawn, standing in cold water with a kind of patience that no customer who calls him for an emergency repair would ever suspect he possessed. These are not exceptions to be noted and then filed away as anomalies. They are the *rule*—the actual texture of human existence, which never holds still long enough to be captured in a single frame.

Corporate marketers, of course, are not attempting philosophical accuracy. They want conversion rates, click-through data, purchasing patterns. And within that narrow ambition, their categories function well enough. But something is lost in the transaction, something that matters beyond the balance sheet: the recognition of shared human space, the spaces where need and pleasure overlap regardless of demographic bracket. The hunger for connection does not check a box. The relief of laughter does not belong to a single voting bloc. Grief, wonder, the particular ache of a summer evening ending—these are not niche markets. They are the commons, the places where all the separate categories dissolve into something more fundamental: simply being alive, simply being human.

And so when we look at the totality of the American public—not the slice extracted for a campaign, not the segment isolated for a study, but the whole unwieldy, contradictory mass of actual people—what we find is something the demographic models cannot render. It is vast. It is largely uncharted. Like the sky at twilight, caught in that suspended moment between the last documented color of sunset and the first pinprick of a named star, it remains blank in the most profound sense: not empty, but *unwritten*. Full of a complexity that has not yet been—perhaps cannot be—reduced to language, waiting instead to be lived.

# Hugh's American Journey

Hugh had always dreamed of visiting the United States. Growing up in a small village, he spent countless hours reading about American cities, their skylines, and the diverse cultures that made up this vast nation. The stories of American history fascinated him—from the founding fathers to the civil rights movement, each chapter revealing a complex tapestry of struggle and progress.

When Hugh finally saved enough money for his trip, he could hardly contain his excitement. The American landscape, he discovered, was far more varied than he had imagined. From the towering skyscrapers of New York to the vast deserts of Arizona, from the rolling hills of Kentucky to the rugged coastline of Maine, each region offered its own distinct character and charm.

During his travels, Hugh met many American families who welcomed him with genuine hospitality. He learned that the American spirit of independence and innovation wasn't just something he'd read about in books—it was alive in the everyday interactions he witnessed. A diner owner in a small Midwestern town shared stories of her grandparents' immigration story. A young entrepreneur in Silicon Valley spoke passionately about his startup dreams.

Hugh's journey through America taught him that the country was best understood not through statistics or historical dates alone, but through the people who called it home. Each conversation added another layer to his understanding of what it meant to be American—a complex, evolving identity shaped by diverse backgrounds, shared values, and an enduring belief in possibility.

By the time Hugh returned home, he carried with him not just souvenirs and photographs, but a deeper appreciation for the American experience—one that would influence how he viewed the world for years to come.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, lyrical prose poem about how marketing algorithms and demographic data reduce Americans to stereotypes, using long cascading sentences with em-dashes and ampersands.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Sorting

They have made a country of us—a country cut into wedges & percentiles, & called it understanding, called it *insight*, called it knowing-you-better-than-you-know-yourself—as if the zip code were a soul, as if the credit score could weep, as if the click-through rate contained the whole trembling architecture of a Tuesday afternoon when you missed your mother & bought something small & red to fill the missing—& they file this under *impulse purchase, emotional trigger, retarget in 48 hours*—they have built a machine that watches you the way a butcher watches a hanging animal, assessing weight & cut & yield, & calls this personalization, calls this *relevance*, calls this giving you what you want before you know you want it—as though wanting were a fixed star & not a weather system, not a thing that changes with the light, with the hour, with whether or not you slept—

& so you become: 35-54, suburban, moderate income, likely Christian, likely to buy minivans & guilt & anti-aging cream in the same breath, likely to vote a certain way because your neighbor voted that way & your neighbor's lawn is similar to your lawn & the algorithm has decided that lawns are destiny—& you become a cluster, a lookalike audience, a persona named Karen or Brandon or Diane, flattened into a PDF that some intern in Austin will present to a room full of people drinking oat milk lattes, & they will nod, because the data doesn't lie, except it does, except it can't help but lie, being made as it is of averages, of medians, of the crushed-together middle where all your specific griefs & specific joys get pureed into something a spreadsheet can hold—

& meanwhile the actual you—the one who cried at a gas station in Ohio for reasons you couldn't name, who still remembers the smell of your grandmother's kitchen & the particular blue of a childhood bicycle—that you is being converted, right now, into a series of behavioral flags & purchase histories & dwell-time metrics, into *high-value target* or *low engagement, deprioritize*, into a shadow-self that shops without you, that wants without you, that has opinions about mattresses & political candidates & the correct amount of avocado to consume weekly—

& this shadow-self will outlive you, will be sold & resold, updated & refined, long after your actual hands have stopped reaching for anything, long after your actual heart has stopped its particular rhythm no algorithm ever fully captured, though god knows they tried, though god knows they're still trying, refining the model, tightening the net, calling it *service*, calling it *convenience*, calling it, always, *for you*—when what they mean, what they have always meant, is: *we have found a way to make your longing profitable, & we will not stop, we will not stop, we will not stop.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a satirical meditation on consumer culture and surveillance capitalism—one that critiques how corporations and search engines profile ordinary people—ending on a quiet, image-driven note about the sky.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Algorithm Learns My Name

They know I bought the generic ibuprofen twice this month,
know I paused four seconds on an ad for adjustable beds,
know the shape of my 2 a.m. loneliness
better than my mother does.

Somewhere in a server farm in Nevada
a small god is being built from my searches—
*how to fix a relationship, how to fix a leaky faucet,
how to fix the feeling that nothing is fixable*—
and it answers each query
with a coupon.

I am a portfolio of intentions.
I am a heatmap of desire
sold to the highest bidder
who wants to sell me
back to myself,
slightly improved,
30% off.

The targeted ads have started to feel like scripture—
*you searched for grief, here is a mattress.
You searched for meaning, here is a mattress.
Everything, eventually, is a mattress.*

I used to think privacy was a room.
Now I understand it was a lie
I told myself in the room
while the room was listening.

Somewhere, an algorithm has decided
I am "likely to convert"—
into what, it does not say.
A customer. A data point.
A ghost that still clicks.

They have my zip code, my heartbreak,
my browser history at 3 a.m.,
the exact color of my hesitation
when I almost bought the thing
that promised to make me whole.

And yet—

tonight the sky is doing something
no one has monetized yet.
Pink bleeding into a blue
that has no brand name,
no click-through rate,
no algorithm patient enough
to sell it back to me.

The clouds don't know my name.
They drift, unbothered,
unprofiled,
uninterested in what I might buy—

and for a moment
I am only a small mammal
looking up,
unfollowed,
unfollowing,
free.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: In the style of an experimental American poet, write a piece exploring the tension between private individual lives and public/political manipulation, incorporating odd juxtapositions like baton twirlers, nuns, and Hugh Grant.
counterfactuals.output:
**Field Notes from the Parade of Everything**

I.
Somewhere a woman irons a shirt for a man
who will lie on television tonight
about the price of bread, the shape of borders,
the weather in a country she has never seen
except as weather, abstracted, arriving
already labeled *crisis.*

She presses the collar flat.
This is not a metaphor. This is Tuesday.

II.
The baton twirlers rehearse in the parking lot
of the Baptist church, their silver wands
catching light like small distress signals,
a Morse code of glitter no one is reading.
Behind them, on the marquee: GOD BLESS + HALFTIME SHOW.
Somewhere a general watches troop movements
on a screen the size of a football field
and calls it, too, a show.

III.
The nuns are teaching cursive again —
loops like the DNA of an older obedience.
Sister Agnes says *a promise is a shape
you make with your hand and keep making
until it becomes your hand.*
Outside, a motorcade slides past like a black eel
through water made of flags.

IV.
Hugh Grant tips his head in an interview,
that practiced flinch of charm,
the smile that says *forgive me* before any crime
has been named — and isn't that the whole apparatus,
the nation's face doing its little bashful dip
while somewhere a bill is signed
that will take the light bill from someone's hand
and call it *reform*?

We elected the flinch. We reelect it nightly.

V.
Meanwhile: a baton spins upward, catches
the sun for one full rotation of held breath,
a nun crosses herself out of habit not belief,
a president's mouth moves in sync
with words written by someone
who has never twirled anything, never knelt,
never ironed a collar at 6 a.m.
for a man who might not come home changed,
might come home *unchanged*, which is its own
catastrophe, small and domestic
as a flag folded into a triangle
and placed, gently, on a table
no camera is pointed at.

VI.
This is the tension: that my life is small
and specific — a kettle, a bruise shaped like Florida,
a phone call I didn't take —
while somewhere it is being narrated
as *the will of the people,*
plural, abstract, marching
in perfect formation
like girls with silver batons
who only wanted, for one afternoon,
to be dazzling,
to be seen,
to not yet be anyone's evidence.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a stream-of-consciousness prose passage about how 'the American common' is fragmented by targeted marketing and demographic categorization, blending irony with tenderness for ordinary people.
counterfactuals.output:
There was supposed to be a common, once, or we told ourselves there was—some plaza of the mind where the milkman and the judge and the woman folding towels in the basement laundromat all stood shoulder to shoulder under the same flat native light, unbranded, unsorted, just *American*, just *people*, the word wide enough to hold a whole continent of Tuesdays—but somewhere between the radio jingles and the punch-card databases we got split into shelves, into zip codes, into *Households 25–34 with Disposable Income*, into *Empty Nesters, Suburban, Likely to Purchase Recreational Vehicles*, and I think about my aunt who is none of those things and all of those things, who drinks her coffee black and prays for her knees and has never once in her life felt like a segment, a quadrant, a niche, though the mail keeps arriving addressed to Her Demographic, never to Her.

Funny how tender it is, actually, underneath the absurdity — the mail-order catalogue that thinks it knows you, the little envelope that says *Dear Homeowner* like it's trying to court you with a name it invented, and somewhere a marketing analyst in a fluorescent-lit office typed *Homeowner* into a spreadsheet cell believing it was a kindness, a personalization, a way of saying *we see you*, when really what they saw was a mortgage bracket, a buying pattern, the ghost-shape of a wallet — and yet there she is anyway, my aunt, alive underneath the label, watering her one tomato plant on the porch at seven a.m. in her robe, unaware she has been coded as *Value-Conscious Boomer, Likely Grocery Coupon User*, unaware that some algorithm somewhere has already decided what commercials will interrupt her evening news, has already decided she is the kind who wants reverse mortgages and long-term care insurance and floral upholstery, and none of it is wrong exactly, and none of it is her, either.

This is the great American sorting-hat trick — take the common table where everyone used to eat, if such a table ever truly existed outside of a Whitman poem or a Frank Capra dissolve, and cut it into a thousand smaller tables, a table for the soccer moms and a table for the bass-fishing dads and a table for the urban singles with disposable income and a table, God help us, for the *aspirational middle*, as if aspiration were a bracket and not a hunger — and yet at every one of those smaller tables somebody is still just tired, still just hoping the check clears, still just watching their kid do a cartwheel in the yard and feeling for one clean unbranded second that this, this exact evening light on the grass, belongs to no market segment at all.

I keep thinking of the woman at the register, scanning through the demographic of me — my hoodie, my headphones, my coupon app pulled up on a cracked phone screen that some other set of algorithms has already decided sorts me into *Millennial, Cost-Conscious, Streaming Subscriber* — and she says *have a good one* the way people have said it forever, before there were personas, before there were pixels tracking my scroll, before some server somewhere started deciding what grief I'm most likely to monetize, and there's a strange grace in that leftover phrase, *have a good one*, unoptimized, uncapitalized on, just a person wishing another person well because that's what the mouth does when it isn't thinking about conversion rates.

Maybe the common was never a place. Maybe it was always this — the accidental tenderness that leaks out between the categories, the moment the targeted ad glitches and shows you something so wrong for your profile that you laugh out loud on the bus, human, unsorted for half a second, and the guy next to you laughs too, and for that half second you are not *Segment 14B, Prime Audience for Discount Airlines,* you are just two people rattling in a metal box through the same gray morning, commonly, uncommonly, alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary, slightly cynical riff on American identity and consumerism, using unconventional punctuation (& instead of and, dashes), vivid absurd imagery, and a final unresolved, painterly image.
counterfactuals.output:
# American Ligature

We are a nation stitched together with dashes—not commas, not full stops, just these small violent hyphens holding together what should never have touched. Kansas & Los Angeles. The Baptist & the barcode. We pledge allegiance with our hands over our hearts & our eyes on the checkout screen, watching the total climb like a fever.

Somewhere a man is buying a flag made in a country that has never seen one flown. Somewhere a woman weeps at a commercial for pickup trucks because the golden light on the hood looks like grace, looks like something her father almost gave her. We do not worship gods anymore—we worship *availability*. Twenty-four hours. Seven days. The convenience store is our only true cathedral & its fluorescent hum is the closest thing we have to plainsong.

Call it freedom—the right to choose between fourteen flavors of nothing. Call it liberty—the credit limit that expands like a lung, in & out, in & out, until the whole economy is just America breathing through a plastic tube.

We are a people raised on drive-thru & dead reckoning, aimed at a horizon we've mortgaged twice.

And yet—

And yet there is still, some nights, a screen door slapping shut in Ohio, a porch light left on for a son who isn't coming, moths beating themselves gold against the bulb like small drunk stars, & somewhere far off a lawn sprinkler ticking its slow arc across grass no one will remember planting—the water catching the streetlamp, hanging there, unfallen, everything about to be lost & nothing lost yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
